title: A causal theory of anesthetic-induced unconsciousness

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a causal, quantitatively predictive explanation of how anesthetic interventions change conscious experience. It would connect a drug’s molecular actions to changes in brain activity and explain when those changes abolish experience, alter its contents, or permit experience despite an inability to respond. The objective includes explaining the return of experience as anesthesia wears off or is reversed.

Conceptual synthesis: conscious experience, behavioral responsiveness and memory must be treated as distinct outcomes. A person’s inability to answer cannot by itself establish an absence of experience, and a lack of later recall cannot settle whether experience occurred. The proposed theory would explain these relationships rather than define unconsciousness solely through observable behavior or subsequent memory.

The research objective allows different anesthetics to reach relevant brain states through different molecular targets and patterns of activity; it does not require a single common molecular target. Whether their effects ultimately converge on a shared causal process, require several mechanisms, or depend strongly on context is a question for the theory to resolve. The supplied evidence does not independently establish the breadth of differences among anesthetics.

significance.text: Conditional significance: achieving this theory would turn anesthetic manipulation of consciousness into a prospectively predictable causal process. It would explain how a controllable physical intervention changes experience and predict outcomes of specified interventions, rather than merely associate a brain measurement with a clinical state. That explanatory capability would be a fundamental advance spanning anesthesiology, consciousness research, neuroscience, pharmacology and dynamical systems.

A direct consequence would be a principled way to evaluate which molecular and neural changes matter for the loss and return of experience, including cases in which responsiveness and experience diverge. The supplied materials do not establish how much existing practice already achieves comparable prediction, so the magnitude of improvement over present methods remains unquantified.

Conditional downstream possibilities include designing anesthetics around identified mechanisms, informing measures of conscious state and guiding interventions that restore consciousness. Applications to sleep or brain injury would require additional discoveries and validation: an explanation developed under anesthesia would not automatically generalize to other causes of altered consciousness. Nor would explaining experience alone establish pain relief, physiological safety or improved clinical outcomes.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability, as framed by this proposal, is a tested account that quantitatively connects anesthetic exposure, molecular action, neural processes and conscious experience. It must identify causal processes rather than rely only on measurements that accompany drug administration or behavioral unresponsiveness. The supplied review cannot establish that this objective remains unmet across the entire field at the present date; its continuing openness is a research premise requiring further documentation.

Scientific barriers inferred from that objective include separating causal changes from accompanying effects, connecting mechanisms across molecular and cortical scales, and determining whether a model transfers across agents and individuals. A successful theory would need to explain exceptions and specify the conditions under which its predictions hold. Similar observable behavior could otherwise conceal different experiential states, while similar neural measurements could have different meanings in different contexts.

A central measurement barrier is the limited ability to verify subjective experience when communication is unavailable. Human reports provide evidence that must be interpreted in relation to responsiveness and memory; animal recordings cannot directly establish what an animal experiences. Proposed causal experiments therefore need converging measurements and interventions, explicit assumptions linking those measurements to experience, and an account of the uncertainty those assumptions leave.

An engineering challenge inferred from the proposal is to perturb the predicted neural process with enough specificity to distinguish the theory from alternatives. A simulation that reproduces a recorded pattern can establish mechanistic plausibility within that model, but it cannot by itself show that the modeled process causes loss of experience in a living brain. Translating such results into quantitative predictions would also require defined measurement procedures, intervention timing and uncertainty estimates.

current_state.text: The reconciled research attributes a relevant result to Adam J. Eisen, Leo Kozachkov and colleagues in “Propofol anesthesia destabilizes neural dynamics across cortex,” identified there as a Neuron publication dated 21 August 2024, DOI 10.1016/j.neuron.2024.06.011. According to that research summary, recordings from two macaques under propofol showed cortical dynamics consistent with reduced stability, and increasing inhibition in a simulated network produced related effects. These details preserve the reported experimental scope; they were not independently confirmed by the supplied evidence review.

The access history limits what can be concluded from this citation. The research says its author inspected the PubMed abstract and encountered a browser check when attempting linked full text. The later review found that the retained source artifact contained a cookie challenge rather than an abstract or paper. Consequently, the retained scientific content could not verify the paper’s identity, publication details, two-macaque sample, cortical findings or simulation result. The source index’s saved and verified indicators do not resolve that content limitation, and the limitation does not establish that the reported result is false.

If the research summary accurately represents the study, the result offers evidence for a possible propofol-related mechanism involving cortical dynamics. It does not establish a general theory across anesthetics, demonstrate that destabilization causes the absence of experience, or show that increased inhibition in an animal reproduces the simulation’s effects. The distinction between recorded dynamics, a modeled mechanism and subjective experience remains essential.

The supplied materials do not establish a field-wide account of subsequent progress. The review specifically leaves freshness as of 1 November 2026 unresolved because its freshness record is empty; the source index’s retrieval timestamp of 11 November 2026 supplies no additional scientific findings. The dated 2024 report should therefore be assessed at its stated scope, while present-day completion or continuing openness of the broader breakthrough remains unverified.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration framework: before collecting decisive test data, specify quantitative predictions for several mechanistically different anesthetics and multiple patient groups. Predictions should address the loss, alteration and return of experience, including cases where response and later recall diverge. Evaluation should include conditions beyond those used to develop the theory, with explicit uncertainty and a clear account of exceptions. These are proposed criteria, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified quantitative experience predictions generalize across anesthetics and patient groups

completion_criteria.text: Proposed causal demonstration: targeted interventions should change the neural processes identified by the theory and shift available evidence about conscious state in the predicted direction. Experiments should distinguish the predicted mechanism from plausible alternatives and determine whether changes in reports reflect experience, ability to communicate or memory. Human and animal studies could provide complementary evidence, with their different limits on access to subjective experience stated explicitly.
completion_criteria.label: Targeted neural interventions shift conscious-state evidence through predicted mechanisms

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent teams should reproduce the central predictions and intervention effects using sufficiently specified protocols and analyses. Demonstrations should report the agents, doses, populations, physiological conditions and measurement settings actually tested, along with failures and uncertainty. Finite experiments would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries; they could not prove literal universality across all anesthetics, people or conscious states. Clinical deployment would require separate evidence of usefulness and safety.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication reproduces predictions and intervention effects within reported boundaries

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with ANS-02, “A reliable real-time monitor of conscious experience during anesthesia”: a causal theory could identify informative signals and explain when a monitor’s readings should be trusted. A monitor nevertheless requires its own evidence for real-time performance and interpretation. Reliable state estimation would not by itself establish the causal explanation sought by ANS-01, and a successful theory would not automatically produce a deployable monitor.

Conceptual comparison with ANS-04, “Surgical unconsciousness with preserved breathing and circulatory control,” and ANS-06, “Broad, active reversal of general anesthesia”: identifying mechanisms of unconsciousness could guide selective induction or active restoration of conscious state. ANS-04 additionally requires preservation of physiological control; ANS-06 requires an effective reversal intervention across its intended scope. Neither engineering and clinical objective follows automatically from explaining conscious experience.

Conceptual comparison with ANS-03, “A broadly applicable, pain-selective surgical nerve block,” and ANS-07, “Systemic, non-opioid analgesia for severe perioperative pain”: these concepts concern controlling pain through different intervention routes. Their overlap with ANS-01 lies in distinguishing components of the anesthetic state and relating interventions to experience. Explaining or inducing unconsciousness does not establish pain-selective blockade or effective systemic analgesia, and pain relief need not require unconsciousness.

Conceptual comparison with ANS-09, “Mechanism-based prevention of chronic postsurgical pain,” and ANS-10, “Mechanism-guided anesthesia to prevent postoperative brain dysfunction”: all three seek explanations that can guide interventions, but their outcomes and timescales differ. ANS-01 concerns experience during transitions into and out of anesthesia. ANS-09 concerns persistent postoperative pain, while ANS-10 concerns postoperative brain dysfunction. Connections would require evidence linking the relevant mechanisms and outcomes.

Conceptual comparison with ANS-05, “A radically accessible, resilient anesthesia platform for essential surgery,” and ANS-08, “Reliable rescue oxygenation in the difficult airway”: these address delivery resilience and airway rescue, respectively. A causal theory of consciousness might eventually inform an anesthesia platform, but it does not establish affordability, accessibility or operational resilience. Likewise, explaining conscious state does not solve rescue oxygenation. These remain distinct innovations with separate demonstrations of success.

unresolved_issues: The retained source artifact does not independently verify the cited paper’s identity, publication metadata, sample size, experimental findings or simulation result; the research account and review therefore remain unequal in evidentiary access.
The supplied materials do not establish whether a broadly predictive causal theory remains absent as of November 2026, or document subsequent advances after the reported 2024 result.
Whether different anesthetics converge on common causal processes, require several mechanisms or demand context-specific explanations remains open within this proposal.
The relationship between cortical destabilization and conscious experience remains unresolved; association and simulation do not establish the required causal link.
The proposed demonstration framework leaves quantitative success thresholds and methods for adjudicating experience when reports are unavailable to future specification.

brief.title: An explanation of how anesthesia switches off experience
possible: Before receiving anesthesia, you could have predictions of when experience would fade, change or return. These would connect a drug’s effects on molecules to brain activity and experience, including experience that continues while someone cannot respond.
why: For anesthesiologists and consciousness researchers, this would explain how a physical intervention changes experience. It could guide the design of anesthetics, ways to measure conscious states and interventions to restore consciousness.

sources.who: Adam J. Eisen, Leo Kozachkov and colleagues
sources.showed: In two macaques, propofol, an anesthesia drug, made activity in the cortex, the brain’s outer layer, less stable. Increasing inhibition, which suppresses nerve activity, produced similar effects in simulated networks.
sources.quote: We found that neural dynamics were more unstable in unconsciousness compared to the awake state.
sources.cited_for: The work links propofol anesthesia to reduced stability in brain activity.
sources.not_established: It does not show that reduced stability causes experience to disappear or explain other anesthetics.

sources.who: André M. Bastos, Jacob A. Donoghue and colleagues
sources.showed: Stimulating the thalamus, a brain region that regulates cortical activity, restored arousal in anesthetized monkeys and reversed several changes in brain activity.
sources.quote: Thalamic stimulation ‘awakened’ anesthetized NHPs and reversed the electrophysiologic features of unconsciousness.
sources.cited_for: Targeted brain stimulation can reverse arousal and electrical changes associated with propofol anesthesia.
sources.not_established: Restored arousal does not directly establish restored subjective experience or validate a general causal theory.

sources.who: Simone Sarasso, Melanie Boly and colleagues
sources.showed: In 18 volunteers, brain responses to magnetic stimulation remained complex under ketamine, alongside later dream reports. Responses were simpler under propofol and xenon, with no reported experience afterward.
sources.quote: after ketamine they reported long, vivid dreams
sources.cited_for: Brain responses and later reports can differ between anesthetics despite the same inability to respond.
sources.not_established: This small study links measurements to later reports; it does not prove what causes experience or its absence.

sources.showed: In 39 healthy men, dream-like experiences were common in reports after unresponsiveness under propofol or dexmedetomidine, drugs used for anesthesia. Awareness of the surroundings was rare.
sources.quote: whereas awareness, signifying connected consciousness, was rarely reported in either state.
sources.cited_for: Being unable to respond under anesthesia can coexist with later reports of experience.
sources.not_established: Later recall cannot establish every experience that occurred, and results in healthy men do not establish predictions for other groups.

shown: Eisen, Kozachkov and colleagues connected propofol anesthesia with unstable brain activity and reproduced related effects in a simulation. Bastos and colleagues went further experimentally: stimulating a brain region restored arousal during propofol anesthesia. These results identify possible mechanisms without establishing what makes experience disappear.
missing: A tested theory still needs to connect drug exposure, molecular effects, brain activity and experience with numerical predictions.
Experiments still need to separate changes that cause experience to disappear from changes that merely accompany anesthesia.
Predictions still need to hold across different anesthetics and patient groups, including cases where response, experience and memory diverge.

milestones.label: Predictions hold across anesthetics and patient groups
milestones.explanation: Numerical predictions set before testing would have to explain lost, altered and returning experience across drugs and patient groups beyond those studied initially. This would establish how broadly the theory applies.

milestones.label: Targeted brain interventions produce the predicted changes
milestones.explanation: Targeted interventions would have to change the proposed brain process and evidence of experience as predicted, separating experience from communication and memory. This would test whether the mechanism causes the change.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce predictions and intervention effects
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce the predictions and intervention effects under clearly described conditions, including failures and uncertainty. This would establish reliability within the boundaries tested.

uncertain: Different anesthetics may converge on a shared process, act through several mechanisms or require explanations that depend on context.
How to judge experience without communication, and what prediction accuracy would count as success, remain open questions.

page.title: A causal theory of anesthetic-induced unconsciousness
page.definition: A quantitative causal model connects anesthetics’ molecular actions to neural activity and the loss and return of conscious experience. Conscious experience means having any subjective experience, including dreams; the model distinguishes it from behavioral responsiveness and later recall.

goal.need: A study published on 31 May 2023 examined anesthetic unresponsiveness in 39 healthy men receiving dexmedetomidine (n=20) or propofol (n=19), and subsequently examined sleep. Most interviews after either state contained recalled experience. Explaining anesthesia therefore requires an account of experience distinct from responsiveness; negative delayed reports cannot exclude experience.

figures.caption: Recall of experience after experimentally induced unresponsiveness
figures.note: Interviews are repeated observations, not independent participants. The sleep experiment included 37 participants.

statements.context: The institute’s anesthesia fact sheet identifies research on awakening and differences between patients.

statements.body: NIGMS-funded Weill Cornell Medicine programme, award R35GM166071
statements.quote: we will test whether common neurodynamic features—such as moment-to-moment excitation–inhibition coupling and spatiotemporal complexity—are necessary for consciousness and how anesthetics perturb them.
statements.context: Research direction stated in the project summary of the programme beginning on 5 August 2026.

statements.quote: As patients return to consciousness, anesthesiologists typically assess through verbal command-following, yet the neural circuits underlying this transition remain incompletely understood.
statements.context: Society meeting report published on 4 May 2026, rather than a consensus statement.

completion.title: Independent human experiments confirm a causal model of anesthetic changes in conscious experience.
completion.criterion: A published model links anesthetic molecular actions to neural dynamics and prospectively predicts the loss, persistence and return of human conscious experience and its alteration by targeted neural interventions. Independent human experiments across mechanistically different anesthetics corroborate these quantitative predictions under registered endpoints and statistical decision rules. Experience, responsiveness and memory have separate endpoints; absent response or recall alone cannot establish unconsciousness. Validation is limited to the agents, concentrations and populations tested.
completion.set_by: Atlas provisional criterion; no outside body’s completion criterion was located.
completion.basis: Searches of NIGMS programmes, ASA guidance, the IFCN committee report, IARS discussions and registered anesthesia-consciousness protocols found no completion test or required prediction accuracy for an integrated causal theory. This provisional test combines the published mechanistic objective with independent prospective confirmation. It establishes an empirically tested account within stated conditions, rather than proof about unreportable experience.

milestones.title: An anesthetic alters a candidate receptor at concentrations relevant to its in vivo effects.
milestones.criterion: An anesthetic changes receptor function at clinically relevant concentrations. The receptor must occur at relevant anatomical sites; applicable stereoselectivity and structure–activity relationships must agree with behavioral effects. Krasowski and Harrison identify GABAA receptors as meeting their candidate-target criteria for propofol and etomidate. On 2 September 2020, Kim et al. reported a 2.6 Å structure of a human GABAA receptor, an ion channel activated by the neurotransmitter GABA, bound to propofol. These results identify molecular action without establishing why experience disappears.
milestones.set_by: Pharmacological target criteria published by Krasowski and Harrison in 1999; corresponding verification approaches are described by Hemmings et al. in 2019, Box 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: The general anaesthetic must alter the function of the receptor at clinically relevant concentrations.

milestones.title: An unresponsive person has a perturbational complexity index above 0.31.
milestones.criterion: During anesthetic unresponsiveness, the maximum perturbational complexity index (PCI), a dimensionless measure of the complexity of EEG responses to magnetic brain stimulation, exceeds 0.31. The IFCN report describes this cutoff, calibrated in 150 people, as supporting consciousness; low PCI cannot exclude experience. Sarasso et al. (7 December 2015; 18 volunteers) found complex responses and dream reports with ketamine, but low complexity without reports with propofol or xenon.
milestones.set_by: International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology committee, 2023 report, section 3.12.2; an empirical consciousness-detection benchmark, not a criterion for a causal theory.
milestones.threshold_quote: an operational cut-off (PCI*=0.31) above which consciousness is invariably present.

milestones.title: Thalamic stimulation raises propofol-anesthetized macaques’ mean wake-up scores above 2 of 6.
milestones.criterion: With propofol infusion maintained, 180 Hz central-thalamic stimulation for 28.5 s produces mean wake-up scores above 2/6. The score combines eye opening, air-puff responses and body movement. The report of 27 April 2021 included two macaques and 22 stimulation sessions; subjective experience was not established. Eisen et al. (21 August 2024; two macaques) measured propofol-associated cortical instability and modeled increased inhibition, without experimentally establishing that instability causes loss of experience.
milestones.set_by: Bastos et al., Massachusetts Institute of Technology, published propofol–macaque stimulation protocol, Figure 8 and Methods; this is a study-specific arousal threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: A high-current and low-current condition was individually titrated per monkey for producing scores on average above or below a wake-up score of 2.

milestones.title: A molecular-to-neural model predicts human experience changes caused by a neural intervention.
milestones.criterion: For a specified anesthetic and population, a model connecting molecular action to neural dynamics correctly predicts the change in reported experience caused by a targeted neural intervention while anesthetic exposure is held constant. A prospective human experiment corroborates that prediction under its registered endpoint and statistical decision rule, assessing responsiveness and memory separately. This is initial human causal validation; independent confirmation across drug mechanisms remains the completion test. No published numerical accuracy threshold was located.
milestones.set_by: Atlas provisional criterion; searches of NIGMS programme objectives and registered anesthesia-consciousness protocols found no accepted benchmark for this integrated human causal test.

not_found: No independently validated model connecting molecular actions, neural interventions and human experience across anesthetic mechanisms was located.
No agreed test certifying absent experience when neither communication nor recall is available was located.
The supplied Sarasso PDF timed out; its institutional repository abstract was accessible.

results.finding: In 2 propofol-anesthetized macaques, cortical response timescales were nearly twice as slow as when awake.
results.detail: A simulation linked increased inhibition to network instability, but the study did not prospectively predict human experience after a targeted neural intervention. Eye closure and opening were used as proxies for consciousness.
results.quote: We discovered that during anesthetic unconsciousness, the response timescales were nearly twice as slow as during the awake state.

results.finding: In 2 propofol-anesthetized macaques, high-current thalamic stimulation produced mean wake-up scores above 2/6.
results.detail: Across 22 stimulation sessions, 180 Hz central-thalamic stimulation was applied for 28.5 seconds while propofol infusion continued. The score measured behavioral arousal; subjective experience was not established.
results.quote: A high-current and low-current condition was individually titrated per monkey for producing scores on average above or below a wake-up score of 2.

results.finding: Six ketamine-anesthetized volunteers had a maximum PCI of 0.55 during unresponsiveness.
results.detail: PCI ranged from 0.35 to 0.55. All six participants reported dreams after emergence.
results.quote:
On the other hand, ketamine-induced unresponsive-
ness was characterized by high PCI values (mean: 0.44, range:
0.35 to 0.55), comparable to those obtained during wakefulness
(ketamine experiment mean: 0.48, range: 0.41 to 0.58; p > 0.05).

results.finding: In cultured mouse hippocampal neurons (sample size not stated), 2 µM propofol prolonged inhibitory synaptic current decay 2.3-fold.
results.detail: The study examined clinically used concentrations and hippocampal GABAA receptors, but the supplied text does not establish whether applicable stereoselectivity and structure–activity relationships agree with behavioral effects.
results.quote: Propofol (2 microM) prolonged the decay time of mlPSCs to an extent similar to which it increased the open probability of GABA- activated channels (2.3- vs 3-fold).

results.finding: 27 propofol analogs showed matching anesthetic activity in tadpoles and activity at recombinant GABAA receptors.
results.detail: The study supports a structure–activity relationship between receptor effects and tadpole behavior, but the text does not establish clinically relevant concentrations or receptor occurrence at relevant anatomical sites.
results.quote: Fourteen of the propofol analogs produced loss of righting reflex in the tadpoles, whereas 13 were inactive as anesthetics. The same pattern of activity was noted with the actions of the compounds at the GABA(A) alpha(1)beta(2)gamma(2s) receptor.

results.finding: Human α1β2γ2 GABAA receptor bound to propofol resolved at 2.6 Å; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The structure identifies propofol binding sites and bears on its molecular action. The reported structural experiment does not establish a functional change at a clinically relevant concentration or the required behavioral relationships.
results.quote:
We obtained structures of the α1β2γ2 GABA
A
receptor in complex with etomidate (3.5 Å) and propofol (2.6 Å) to directly interrogate binding interactions and provide a foundation for understanding allosteric potentiation.
